What remains when everything fades?

This is not a question with an easy answer. It is the question that drives this book: through the void of infinite duration, the burden of immortal existence, and the unsettling possibility that reality itself may be shaped by the minds that perceive it.

The Malleable Eternity explores what happens when consciousness confronts infinity. Drawing on Plato, Nietzsche, and Sartre, and on contemporary thinkers such as David Chalmers, Derek Parfit, and Nick Bostrom, it challenges the assumption that eternity is a fixed state and proposes that it may be something we can shape.

Inside you will discover

  • A thought experiment that follows a single consciousness across one million years, and the haunting wish to be mortal again
  • The Ship of Theseus applied to brain uploading: if your mind is copied, does the original survive?
  • Why immortality without meaning may not be a gift, but a sentence
  • The simulation hypothesis: are we already inside a system we did not create?
  • Whether artificial intelligence can ever truly wake up, or will remain forever unconscious of itself
  • The uncomfortable possibility that reality never needed us at all

A book of questions

This is not a book of answers. It is a book of questions that philosophers, scientists, and seekers have asked for millennia, now reframed for an age of AI, digital twins, and quantum uncertainty. It asks not only what exists, but how existence becomes malleable once humanity takes on the role of co-architect of being.

For readers of Reality+ by David Chalmers, Life 3.0 by Max Tegmark, and The Precipice by Toby Ord.

Perhaps there are no final answers. But you will keep asking. And that may be the only eternity that matters.

Continue the series: Volume 2, The Ghosts of Time, leaves the thought experiment behind and turns to the observable world: companies, religions, and languages as evidence that spirit is not bound to matter.

Excerpt: Foreword · approx. 3 min read

What remains when everything else fades away?

For centuries, philosophers, scientists, and mystics have sought the truth about our existence. They have asked whether reality is what it appears to be, whether consciousness is merely a function of the brain or something more fundamental, and whether our universe represents the whole of existence or merely a fragment of something vaster. These questions have no settled answers—but the asking itself reveals something essential about the human condition.

In this book, we embark on a journey to the outermost edges of understanding. We do not only examine the nature of eternity, but also the role of consciousness in shaping reality. This exploration challenges traditional philosophy, stretching beyond the confines of what we assume to be possible.

A Journey into the Unknown

Imagine existing in a state where time does not flow—no past, no future, only an endless now. In such a state, identity itself becomes precarious. Without external reference points, without the rhythm of change, the mind might stagnate into numbness or transform into something entirely unrecognizable.

The human experience is fundamentally shaped by change. We measure life in cycles, beginnings and endings, growth and decay, past and future. But in an eternal state, where nothing moves forward or backward, where does meaning come from? Without time, without limitations, without a clear sense of progress, does identity persist, or does it dissolve into the void?

These questions lead us beyond the boundaries of traditional philosophy. We will dive into the thoughts of Plato, Nietzsche, Sartre, and Diogenes, explore modern theories of quantum mechanics, and ask whether artificial intelligence could one day develop true self-awareness. What if consciousness itself is not bound to organic life? Could an AI, left to evolve indefinitely, become something akin to a soul?

The lines between reality, perception, and intelligence blur when one contemplates infinity.

Reality as an Illusion?

Some of the greatest thinkers of our time question whether what we perceive as “reality” is real at all. Is our world a physical certainty, or is it merely a simulation, a mathematical structure that only collapses into form through observation and consciousness?

Quantum mechanics has revealed something strange: according to certain interpretations, observation appears to affect the behavior of particles. Before measurement, particles seem to exist in superposition—multiple states at once. While physicists debate what this truly means, some philosophers have asked a provocative question: What if consciousness itself plays a role in determining what becomes real?

We arrive at a fundamental paradox: If reality is shaped by perception, can we ever truly understand what exists beyond our own awareness?

The connection between perception, existence, and the malleability of reality is the central theme of this book. It does not merely propose hypotheses; it challenges the reader to question their very understanding of reality.

We will explore the possibility that reality is not a fixed structure, but a formless sea of possibilities, molded by consciousness. We will challenge the assumption that time is linear, that intelligence is limited to organic beings, and that our universe exists as an objective truth.

Beyond the Final Answer

If we push beyond the familiar, beyond the structured reality we take for granted, we may find that the ultimate truth is not an answer, but a question. Perhaps reality is not something we uncover, but something we create.

What happens when consciousness is no longer bound by time?
What does it mean to exist in a state of infinite possibility?
Does eternity reveal the nature of reality, or does it obscure it?

It may be that there are no final answers.
But maybe that’s exactly the point.

About the author

Asterios Raptis is a philosopher, author, and software developer at the intersection of technology and metaphysics. Born in Germany and raised with Greek roots, he combines classical philosophy with contemporary science and philosophy of mind, and writes for readers who refuse to accept easy answers about existence.
